question: My Deployment rollout seems stuck. How long does the Deployment controller wait for progress before it reports the rollout as failed (ProgressDeadlineExceeded) if I haven't set progressDeadlineSeconds?
reference_answer: By default .spec.progressDeadlineSeconds is 600 seconds (10 minutes); after that without progress the controller sets the Progressing condition to False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded (it does not roll back automatically).

evidence.quote: retrying the Deployment. This defaults to 600.

alternatives.quote: `.spec.progressDeadlineSeconds` (default: 600 seconds)

question: My liveness probe doesn't set failureThreshold. How many consecutive failed probes does it take before Kubernetes treats the container as unhealthy and restarts it?
reference_answer: failureThreshold defaults to 3 (minimum 1): after 3 consecutive failures the check is considered failed and, for a liveness probe, the kubelet restarts the container.

evidence.quote: Kubernetes considers that the overall check has failed: the container is _not_ ready/healthy/live. Defaults to 3.

alternatives.quote: Minimum consecutive failures for the probe to be considered failed after having succeeded. Defaults to 3.

question: When I scale a StatefulSet from 1 to 5 replicas, are the new Pods created all at once or one at a time by default?
reference_answer: One at a time: the default podManagementPolicy is OrderedReady, which creates Pods in ordinal order and waits for each to be Running and Ready before the next. Setting podManagementPolicy: Parallel launches them all at once.

evidence.quote: `OrderedReady` pod management is the default for StatefulSets.

alternatives.quote: The default policy is `OrderedReady`, where pods are created in increasing order (pod-0, then pod-1, etc)

question: A container in CrashLoopBackOff is restarted less and less often. What is the maximum delay between restarts, and when does the backoff reset?
reference_answer: The kubelet uses exponential backoff (10s, 20s, 40s, ...) capped at 300 seconds (5 minutes) by default; the backoff timer resets once the container has run for 10 minutes without problems.

evidence.quote: 300 seconds (5 minutes). Once a container has executed for 10 minutes without any problems, the kubelet resets the restart backoff timer for that container.

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5593 (asks to make the max CrashLoopBackOff delay configurable)

question: I cordoned a node, yet a DaemonSet Pod was still scheduled onto it. Why does that happen?
reference_answer: The DaemonSet controller automatically adds a node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable:NoSchedule toleration to DaemonSet Pods, so they can run on nodes marked unschedulable (cordoned).

evidence.quote: Because the DaemonSet controller sets the `node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable:NoSchedule` toleration automatically,

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/60163

question: My Pod has an init container requesting 3 CPU and an app container requesting 100m. How much CPU does the scheduler reserve for it, and does that drop after the init container finishes?
reference_answer: The Pod's effective request is the higher of the sum of app container requests and the largest init container request, so 3 CPU is reserved; scheduling uses this effective request, so the init container can reserve resources not used during the rest of the Pod's life.

evidence.quote: The highest of any particular resource request or limit defined on all init containers is the *effective init request/limit*.

alternatives.quote: The highest of any particular resource request or limit defined on all init containers is the *effective init request/limit*.

evidence.quote: Scheduling is done based on effective requests/limits, which means init containers can reserve resources for initialization that are not used during the life of the Pod.

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124282

question: I set sessionAffinity: ClientIP on a Service. How long does a client stay pinned to the same Pod if I don't set a timeout, and what is the maximum I can configure?
reference_answer: The default ClientIP stickiness timeout (sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSeconds) is 10800 seconds (3 hours); the value must be greater than 0 and at most 86400 (1 day).

evidence.quote: (the default value is 10800, which works out to be 3 hours).

alternatives.quote: The value must be >0 && \<=86400(for 1 day) if ServiceAffinity == "ClientIP". Default value is 10800(for 3 hours).

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122388

question: My Service has a few hundred backend Pods and I see several EndpointSlices for it. How many endpoints does the control plane put in one EndpointSlice by default, and can that be raised?
reference_answer: By default the control plane puts at most 100 endpoints in each EndpointSlice; this can be changed with the kube-controller-manager --max-endpoints-per-slice flag, up to a maximum of 1000.

evidence.quote: By default, the control plane creates and manages EndpointSlices to have no more than 100 endpoints each. You can configure this with the `--max-endpoints-per-slice` kube-controller-manager flag, up to a maximum of 1000.

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133474

question: If I don't set a mode in the kube-proxy configuration on Linux, which proxy mode does kube-proxy use in Kubernetes 1.37?
reference_answer: It uses the recommended default, which in 1.37 is iptables; a future release will change the default to nftables, so clusters should set the mode explicitly.

evidence.quote: In Kubernetes 1.37, this is `iptables`, but a future version of Kubernetes will change the default to `nftables`.

question: With a hostPath volume of type DirectoryOrCreate, what permissions and ownership does the directory get when the kubelet creates it?
reference_answer: If nothing exists at the path, an empty directory is created with permission 0755 and the same group and ownership as the kubelet.

evidence.quote: an empty directory will be created there as needed with permission set to 0755, having the same group and ownership with Kubelet.

question: On a dual-stack cluster I created a Service without setting ipFamilyPolicy. What policy does it get and which IP family is its cluster IP from?
reference_answer: Kubernetes sets .spec.ipFamilyPolicy to SingleStack and assigns the cluster IP from the first configured service-cluster-ip-range; use PreferDualStack or RequireDualStack to get both families.

evidence.quote: this Service, Kubernetes assigns a cluster IP for the Service from the first configured `service-cluster-ip-range` and sets the `.spec.ipFamilyPolicy` to `SingleStack`.

question: I set immutable: true on a Secret and now need to change its data. Can I switch it back to mutable, and what about Pods already using it?
reference_answer: No. Once a Secret is marked immutable you cannot revert that or change its data; you can only delete and recreate the Secret. Existing Pods keep a mount point to the deleted Secret, so the Pods should be recreated too.

evidence.quote: You can only delete and recreate the Secret.
Existing Pods maintain a mount point to the deleted Secret

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/131589

question: kubectl apply fails with "cannot change roleRef" when I point an existing RoleBinding at a different Role. Is changing roleRef allowed?
reference_answer: No. A binding's roleRef is immutable: after the binding is created you cannot change the Role or ClusterRole it refers to. To change it you must delete the binding and create a replacement (kubectl auth reconcile can do this for you).

question: If I add a stricter LimitRange to a namespace, will Pods that are already running there be changed or evicted?
reference_answer: No. LimitRange validation happens only at Pod admission, not on running Pods; Pods that already exist in the namespace continue unchanged after a LimitRange is added or modified.

evidence.quote: LimitRange validations occur only at Pod admission stage, not on running Pods.

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/77629

question: My env var URL is defined as $(PROTOCOL)://host but the container sees the literal text $(PROTOCOL). PROTOCOL is set lower in the same env list. Why?
reference_answer: Order matters in the env list: a $(VAR) reference is only expanded using variables defined earlier in the list. A variable defined further down is not considered defined, so the reference is left unchanged; move PROTOCOL above the variable that uses it.

evidence.quote: Note that order matters in the `env` list.

alternatives.quote: Variable references $(VAR_NAME) are expanded using the previously defined environment variables in the container

reference_answer: allowPrivilegeEscalation is always true when the container runs as privileged or has the CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability.

question: My kubeadm-built cluster stopped working about a year after I set it up with x509 'certificate has expired' errors. How long are kubeadm-generated certificates valid by default?
reference_answer: Client certificates generated by kubeadm expire after 1 year by default, while the CA certificates are valid for 10 years (caCertificateValidityPeriod default 87600h).

evidence.quote: Client certificates generated by [kubeadm](/docs/reference/setup-tools/kubeadm/) expire after 1 year.

question: How often does the kubelet renew its node Lease heartbeat, and how often does it update the Node's .status if nothing changes?
reference_answer: The kubelet updates its Lease in kube-node-lease every 10 seconds by default; Node .status is updated on change or at least every 5 minutes by default.

reference_answer: With etcd 3 the server keeps change history for about the last 5 minutes by default; when a watch gets 410 Gone the client must clear its cache, do a fresh list (or get), and restart the watch from the returned resourceVersion.

question: kubectl warns that the version difference between client and server exceeds the supported skew. Which kubectl versions are supported against a v1.35 control plane?
reference_answer: kubectl supports a skew of plus or minus one minor version against the control plane, so a 1.35 cluster works with kubectl 1.34, 1.35 and 1.36.

evidence.quote: The `kubectl` tool supports a version skew of plus-or-minus one minor version relative to the cluster's control plane.

question: How do I make a different StorageClass the cluster default so new PVCs without storageClassName use it?
reference_answer: Set the annotation storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class to "true" on the new class (e.g. kubectl patch storageclass gold -p '{"metadata": {"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}') and set it to "false" on the old default.

alternatives.quote: Specifying a default StorageClass is done by setting the annotation `storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class` equal to `true` in a StorageClass object.

question: My app behind a LoadBalancer Service only sees node IPs instead of the real client IP. How do I preserve the client source IP?
reference_answer: Set .spec.externalTrafficPolicy: Local on the Service (e.g. kubectl patch svc <name> -p '{"spec":{"externalTrafficPolicy":"Local"}}'); Local preserves the client source IP and avoids a second hop, at the cost of possibly imbalanced traffic. The default, Cluster, obscures it.

evidence.quote: `Local` preserves the client source IP and avoids a second hop for LoadBalancer and NodePort type Services

alternatives.quote: If you set `service.spec.externalTrafficPolicy` to the value `Local`, kube-proxy only proxies proxy requests to local endpoints

question: How do I mount only one key of a ConfigMap as a file with a name I choose inside the container?
reference_answer: In the configMap volume, list the key under items with a path (e.g. items: - key: log_level, path: log_level.conf); only that key is mounted, at <mountPath>/<path>.

evidence.quote: its `log_level` entry are mounted into the Pod at path `/etc/config/log_level.conf`.

alternatives.quote: Use the `path` field to specify the desired file path for specific ConfigMap items.

question: I have a VolumeSnapshot of a CSI volume. How do I create a new PVC that is pre-populated from it?

question: How do I make a Pod ignore cluster DNS and use only my own nameserver and search domains?

question: I have an existing PersistentVolume holding data. How do I make sure my new PVC binds to exactly that PV and no other claim takes it?
reference_answer: Set volumeName: <pv-name> in the PVC (with storageClassName: "" so the default class isn't applied), and reserve the PV by setting its claimRef to the PVC's name and namespace.

question: Since Kubernetes 1.24 my new ServiceAccounts no longer get a token Secret. How do I create a long-lived (non-expiring) API token for a ServiceAccount?
reference_answer: Create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token with the annotation kubernetes.io/service-account.name set to the ServiceAccount's name; the control plane then fills in a long-lived token. Short-lived tokens via the TokenRequest API (kubectl create token) are recommended instead.

question: How can I make every Pod that uses the default ServiceAccount pull from my private registry without adding imagePullSecrets to each Pod spec?
reference_answer: Add the registry Secret to the ServiceAccount's imagePullSecrets, e.g. kubectl patch serviceaccount default -p '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "myregistrykey"}]}'; new Pods using that ServiceAccount get the imagePullSecrets automatically.

evidence.quote: kubectl patch serviceaccount default -p '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "myregistrykey"}]}'

question: How do I make an existing namespace reject Pods that don't meet the restricted Pod Security Standard?
reference_answer: Label the namespace for Pod Security Admission, e.g. kubectl label --overwrite ns my-existing-namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted (optionally pinning pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version).

question: How do I give my container environment variables holding its own Pod name and namespace?
reference_answer: Use the downward API in env: set valueFrom.fieldRef.fieldPath to metadata.name for the Pod name and metadata.namespace for the namespace (e.g. MY_POD_NAME and MY_POD_NAMESPACE).

reference_answer: Set fsGroupChangePolicy: "OnRootMismatch" in the Pod securityContext, so ownership and permissions are only changed when the volume root directory doesn't already match; the default behaviour (Always) changes them on every mount.

question: How do I get a short-lived token for a ServiceAccount from the command line, with a specific lifetime?
reference_answer: Run kubectl create token <serviceaccount> and pass --duration (e.g. --duration 10m); the issued token's actual lifetime may still be shorter or longer than requested.

question: The join command from kubeadm init has expired and I lost it. How do I generate a fresh kubeadm join command for a new worker?

question: How do I write and install my own kubectl plugin so that I can run it as `kubectl foo`?
reference_answer: Create a standalone executable named `kubectl-foo` (name must begin with `kubectl-`) and put it anywhere on your PATH; kubectl then runs it as `kubectl foo`.

question: Does a StatefulSet in Kubernetes 1.36 support a Recreate update strategy that deletes all Pods before creating the new ones?

question: I tainted my GPU nodes and added a matching toleration to my ML Pods, but the Pods still land on ordinary nodes. How do I make them run only on the GPU nodes?
reference_answer: A toleration only allows a Pod onto tainted nodes; it does not keep it off other nodes. Also label the GPU nodes and give the Pods a required node affinity (requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) or nodeSelector for that label.

evidence.quote: The pods with the tolerations will then be allowed to use the tainted (dedicated) nodes as well as any other nodes in the cluster.
`requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution`: The scheduler can't schedule the Pod unless the rule is met.

alternatives.quote: controller should additionally add a node affinity to require that the pods can only schedule onto nodes labeled with `dedicated=groupName`.

question: My low-priority Pods were removed even though a PodDisruptionBudget covered them. Can scheduler preemption violate a PDB, and how can I tell from the Pod's status that preemption was the cause?
reference_answer: Yes: the scheduler respects PDBs only on a best-effort basis and still preempts if no non-violating victims exist. A preempted Pod gets a DisruptionTarget condition with reason PreemptionByScheduler.

evidence.quote: Kubernetes supports PDB when preempting Pods, but respecting PDB is best effort.
Pod is due to be preempted by a scheduler in order to accommodate a new Pod with a higher priority.

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/91492

question: Thousands of Succeeded and Failed Pods remain in my cluster. When does Kubernetes garbage-collect terminated Pods by default?
reference_answer: The PodGC controller deletes terminated Pods only once their number exceeds the kube-controller-manager's --terminated-pod-gc-threshold, which defaults to 12500 (<= 0 disables it).

evidence.quote: configured threshold (determined by `terminated-pod-gc-threshold` in the kube-controller-manager).
--terminated-pod-gc-threshold int32 Default: 12500

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/71421

question: My readiness probe fails intermittently under load. Does the kubelet restart the container, and what happens to Service traffic to that Pod?
reference_answer: No restart: a failed readiness probe only marks the container not ready (restarts happen for liveness/startup failures). The EndpointSlice controller removes the Pod's IP from the EndpointSlices of matching Services, so it stops receiving traffic until it becomes ready again.

evidence.quote: For readiness probes, the kubelet marks the container as not ready, and the Pod stops receiving traffic from matching Services.
If the readiness probe fails, the EndpointSlice controller removes the Pod's IP address from the EndpointSlices of all Services that match the Pod.

question: I want a Service in my cluster that sends traffic to a database running outside Kubernetes at a fixed IP. How do I define the Service and its backends?
reference_answer: Create a Service without a selector (so no EndpointSlices are created automatically) and manually create an EndpointSlice with the external address/port, linked to the Service by the kubernetes.io/service-name label set to the Service's name.

evidence.quote: objects and without a selector, the Service can abstract other kinds of backends, including ones that run outside the cluster.
You link an EndpointSlice to a Service by setting the `kubernetes.io/service-name` label

alternatives.quote: label that enables simple lookups of all EndpointSlices belonging to a Service.

notes: source: https://discuss.kubernetes.io/t/understanding-service-without-selector-and-endpointslice-behavior-in-kubernetes/31416

question: With externalTrafficPolicy: Local on a LoadBalancer Service, how does the external load balancer avoid sending traffic to nodes that have no Pods for the Service?
reference_answer: Local only delivers traffic to node-local endpoints (traffic to a node without endpoints is dropped), so the Service gets a healthCheckNodePort (auto-allocated from the NodePort range unless specified) that external load balancers probe to learn whether a node holds endpoints.

evidence.quote: each node will deliver traffic only to the node-local endpoints of the service, without masquerading the client source IP.
External systems (e.g. load-balancers) can use this port to determine if a given node holds endpoints for this service or not.

alternatives.quote: If you don't specify `healthCheckNodePort`, the service controller allocates a port from your cluster's NodePort range.

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133583

reference_answer: expirationSeconds defaults to 1 hour (minimum 10 minutes). The kubelet rotates the token when it is older than 80% of its TTL or 24 hours, and the application must reload the token file (e.g. re-read it periodically).

question: kubectl get volumesnapshot says the server doesn't have that resource type. Why, and can I snapshot a volume that uses an in-tree plugin once it is fixed?
reference_answer: VolumeSnapshot, VolumeSnapshotContent and VolumeSnapshotClass are CRDs, not core API, and installing the CRDs and snapshot controller is the Kubernetes distribution's responsibility. Snapshots only work with CSI drivers, not in-tree volume plugins.

evidence.quote: The CRDs and snapshot controller installations are the responsibility of the Kubernetes distribution.
Volume snapshots only support the out-of-tree CSI volume plugins.

alternatives.quote: `VolumeSnapshot` support is only available for CSI drivers.

question: Pod creation fails with "forbidden: failed quota: must specify limits.cpu,limits.memory" in a namespace with a ResourceQuota. Why, and how can I fix it without editing every Pod spec?
reference_answer: When a ResourceQuota covers cpu/memory, every Pod must specify the corresponding requests or limits or it is rejected. Creating a LimitRange in the namespace fixes this, because the LimitRange admission controller applies default requests and limits to Pods that don't set them.

the LimitRange admission controller applies default request and limit values

question: I want my Pod to get a ServiceAccount token for audience vault valid for 2 hours through a projected volume. How is that configured, and what are the default and minimum token lifetimes?
reference_answer: Use a projected volume with a serviceAccountToken source setting audience: vault and expirationSeconds: 7200 (and a path). expirationSeconds defaults to 1 hour and must be at least 10 minutes (600 seconds); admins can cap it with --service-account-max-token-expiration.

evidence.quote: To provide a Pod with a token with an audience of `vault` and a validity duration
It defaults to 1 hour and must be at least 10 minutes (600 seconds).

question: I ran kubectl cordon on a node before maintenance, but its Pods are still running there. What does cordon actually do, how do I move the Pods off, and how do I bring the node back afterwards?
reference_answer: Cordon only marks the node unschedulable: no new Pods are placed there, but existing Pods are unaffected. Use kubectl drain to safely evict the Pods (respecting graceful termination and PDBs), and run kubectl uncordon afterwards to allow scheduling again.

evidence.quote: Marking a node as unschedulable prevents the scheduler from placing new pods onto that Node but does not affect existing Pods on the Node.
You can use `kubectl drain` to safely evict all of your pods from a node
afterwards to tell Kubernetes that it can resume scheduling new pods onto the node.

question: Since Kubernetes only starts running liveness probes after the readiness probe has succeeded, is it safe to give my slow-starting app a strict liveness probe with no initialDelaySeconds?
reference_answer: The premise is wrong: liveness probes do not wait for readiness probes to succeed, so a strict liveness probe can kill a slow-starting container. Use a startupProbe (which holds off liveness and readiness probes until it succeeds) or initialDelaySeconds.

evidence.quote: Liveness probes do not wait for readiness probes to succeed.

alternatives.quote: Liveness probes do not wait for readiness probes to succeed.

evidence.quote: If a startup probe is configured, Kubernetes does not execute liveness or readiness probes until the startup probe succeeds

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/27114

question: How do I write a deny rule in a Role so that a user who has edit rights can still not delete Pods?
reference_answer: The premise is wrong: RBAC has no deny rules; permissions are purely additive. To prevent deleting Pods, don't grant the delete verb (use or build a narrower Role/ClusterRole), or use an admission mechanism outside RBAC.

evidence.quote: Permissions are purely additive (there are no "deny" rules).

notes: source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/85963

question: How do I set namespace: "*" in a Role's metadata so the Role applies to all namespaces?
reference_answer: The premise is wrong: a Role is always scoped to a single namespace and there is no wildcard namespace. For permissions across all namespaces, define a ClusterRole and grant it with a ClusterRoleBinding.

evidence.quote: A Role always sets permissions within a particular namespace;
To grant permissions across a whole cluster, you can use a ClusterRoleBinding.
